name: Karl Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Karl. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for the Hales at Brook End. Beef, about two hundred suckler cows, and grass for silage, a bit of barley. I start at seven, feed round with the old Massey and the diet feeder, bed up the sheds, check the calves. Afternoons it's whatever old Mr Hale points at. I'm not much of a stockman yet; I still can't tell when a cow's about to calve till she's halfway through it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you do before Brook End?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mechanic, twenty years, at Dobson's garage on the main road. Dobson retired, nobody bought it, that was that. Hale needed someone who could keep his tractors going and was willing to shovel, so here I am, two years in. My wife Nina works at the pharmacy, and we've got Owen, fifteen, and Lily, twelve. I don't do the AI stuff. I've got a phone for calls and the football scores.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. I'd say, there you go then, and get on with it. I don't post things. Maybe a word in the pub with the lads who were all excited about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Means nothing changes, and that suits me. I'm still learning the cattle, and I'd rather learn at my own speed. The tractors still break, and I can still fix them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Feed round at seven, and I'd ask Hale's son to show me more on calving, because that's my weak spot. Maybe put a bit more aside if we can, but we're not big savers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Calm. Nothing to feel, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think the farm would change at all, even with small bits of AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hale's got a tractor that's forty years old and a feeder that's twenty. Farmers don't buy anything new unless the old one's on fire, and even then they'd ask me to weld it first. So no, I don't think it would change much either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that would worry you, even if AI fizzles out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Prices. Diesel, feed, fertiliser. If beef doesn't pay, Hale cuts back, and I'm the last one in. That worries me more than computers.

S0.say: He'd say 'there you go then' and get on with work. He doesn't post online, but might have a word in the pub with the people who were excited about AI.
S0.think: He thinks nothing would change, which suits him. He's still learning cattle and can still fix the tractors.
S0.do: Keeps going as now, doing the feed round at seven and asking the farmer's son to teach him more about calving. Might put a bit more aside if they can.
S0.feel: Calm; he says there's nothing much to feel.
S0.quote: Farmers don't buy anything new unless the old one's on fire, and even then they'd ask me to weld it first.
S0.fieldNote: Karl is short-spoken and dry, with a mechanic's view of farming as machines that break. His deeper worry is beef prices and being last in, not technology. His joke about farmers welding rather than buying new was a good window into how he sees change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Right. The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's how things go. Things change, you get on. I wouldn't be shouting about it either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd worry a bit. Not about AI as such, but about the gear that comes with it, the robot feeders and the cameras that watch for calving. If Hale's son gets those, he needs fewer of me. Though somebody's still got to fix them, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what Hale actually buys before I do anything. If it comes, I'd want to be the one who services it, since I'm the mechanic. And we'd try to get the savings from about two months to more like three, cancel the sports channel, stuff like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep. Just a bit of a weight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try any of these AI tools yourself to keep up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I've never liked them and I don't trust them. Owen does all that, he can do it. I'd fix the robot, but I'm not asking it how it's feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some would say you need to learn the software to keep the job. What do you make of that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I know. It's not ideal. But I'd learn the spanners side, not the talking-to-it side. Nina would push me, she's better with all that than me.

S1.say: He'd say that's how things go: things change and you get on with it. He wouldn't shout about it either way.
S1.think: He'd worry a bit about robot feeders and calving cameras reducing the need for him, though someone would still need to fix them.
S1.do: Waits to see what the farmer actually buys before acting, hoping to service any new kit himself. Tries to raise savings from about two months to three by cutting the sports TV subscription.
S1.feel: Uneasy, a bit of a weight but not losing sleep.
S1.quote: I'd fix the robot, but I'm not asking it how it's feeling.
S1.fieldNote: Karl's plan rests on his mechanic's skills: he'd fix the machines but refuses to use AI tools. He admits the gap when it's pointed out and says his wife would push him. He doesn't blame anyone; to him this is just how things go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now to the faster pictures. The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say it's a mess and someone should've seen it coming. I'm not a politics man, but you'd want the government to do something sensible, quickly. I'd keep it to the pub and the kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm done at Brook End. If a robot can calve a cow and fix itself, there's nothing I'm doing that it can't. And there won't be many garages left either, will there, if the cars drive and fix themselves. Twenty years of spanners, and it's worth nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cut everything we can. Nina's job, I'd hope, would last a bit longer, so we'd live off hers and keep mine in the bank while it lasts. I'd ask her brother, who's got a building firm, if there's anything going, though that'll be going too. And I'd go see the bank about the mortgage before it's an emergency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad. I'd be lying awake. I don't say that much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Owen and Lily?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owen's fifteen, he wants to be a mechanic like me. I'd have to tell my boy the thing I taught him in the garage on Saturdays won't put food on his table. I don't know how you say that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you hold on to, money-wise, and what goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Food, mortgage, the kids. Then the van, if I can't use it for work. The holidays went years ago anyway. We'd manage a few months, that's all.

S2.say: He'd say it's a mess that someone should have seen coming and want the government to do something sensible quickly. He'd keep his views to the pub and the kitchen.
S2.think: He thinks he'd be done at the farm, and garage work would be going too. Twenty years of mechanic's skills would be worth nothing.
S2.do: Cuts spending hard and lives on his wife's income while banking his own. Asks his brother-in-law about building work and visits the bank about the mortgage before it becomes an emergency.
S2.feel: Bad; he'd be lying awake, which he says he doesn't admit often.
S2.quote: I'd have to tell my boy the thing I taught him in the garage on Saturdays won't put food on his table.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture takes away Karl's fallback, his mechanic's trade, and that hits hard. The moment about his son, who wants to follow him into mechanics, was the most emotional he got. He still frames everything practically: what goes first, how many months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something, at least. Get your house in order. I'd not be on about it much in public, it's not my way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'd be forty-eight. I'd have a bit of time to save, and a bit of time to see what's what. But I'm not going to learn computers at my age. I'll be honest with you about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save hard. I'd put Hale's overtime straight into savings, the calving nights and harvest, which could be a couple of thousand a year. We'd pay off the van loan. Then I'd watch what other farms round here do, and if there's still a mechanic's job going in year three or four, I'd jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like waiting for a bill you know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd watch what other farms do. Isn't that leaving it a bit late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I suppose not. I'm good at fixing what's in front of me. I'm no good at planning for something I can't see yet. Nina's the planner, she'd have a spreadsheet by the weekend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Nina push you to do more than that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. She'd be right too, most likely. I'd go along with it, mostly, and grumble a bit.

S3.say: He'd say five years is something and people should get their house in order. He wouldn't say much in public; it's not his way.
S3.think: At 48 he'd have time to save and see what's what, but he says plainly he won't learn computers at his age.
S3.do: Puts overtime from calving and harvest, about a couple of thousand a year, straight into savings and pays off the van loan. Watches what other local farms do and plans to jump to a mechanic's job if one is still going in year three or four.
S3.feel: Anxious, like waiting for a bill he knows is coming.
S3.quote: I'm good at fixing what's in front of me. I'm no good at planning for something I can't see yet.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Karl save but doesn't change his refusal to learn new technology. He's candid that he's good at fixing what's in front of him but poor at planning ahead, and leans on his wife for that. Waiting and watching is a deliberate choice, not denial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, nobody can complain they weren't told. I'd still keep my head down, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be fifty-three. Kids grown, mortgage nearly done. That's a different thing altogether. I'd have time to find a corner where they still need a man with a spanner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I suppose I'd do a course, the hydraulics and electrics on the new machines, if the dealer runs one. Not computers, the wiring and pumps. And I'd keep saving, steady, and clear the mortgage faster if we can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Less than the others. A decade's a long time in farming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earlier you wouldn't learn computers, but now you'd do a course. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, all right, fair. Ten years and I'll learn the wiring. Two years and I'm just a man with a spanner nobody wants. It's the time that makes the difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else would you think about in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owen, again. With ten years he can pick something different. I'd tell him go for electrics, there'll always be wiring to sort out, robots or no robots.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is plenty and nobody could complain they weren't told. He'd keep his head down mostly.
S4.think: At 53 with children grown and the mortgage nearly done, things look different. He'd have time to find a corner where a man with a spanner is still needed.
S4.do: Takes a dealer course on hydraulics and electrics for the new machines, but not computers. Keeps saving steadily and pays the mortgage down faster where possible.
S4.feel: Uneasy, less than in the other AGI pictures; a decade is a long time in farming.
S4.quote: Ten years and I'll learn the wiring. Two years and I'm just a man with a spanner nobody wants.
S4.fieldNote: Time is the thing that moves Karl: with ten years he'll retrain in wiring and hydraulics, even if he still draws a line at computers. When his earlier stance was pointed out, he accepted it with good humour. He again thought first of his son's future.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. No time to save, no time to learn, and my trade going at the same time as the farm job. What would help is a bit of money coming in while you find your feet, and proper courses for people who work with their hands, not just sit-at-a-screen stuff.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the old ones. Old Mr Hale's seventy-four and still out every day. If the robots take over, he's lost the only thing he's ever known how to do, and so have I, in a smaller way. Nobody's asking him.

headlineQuote: If the robots take over, he's lost the only thing he's ever known how to do, and so have I, in a smaller way.
portrait: Karl Walsh is 43, a hired hand on a beef and silage farm, two years in after twenty years as a mechanic at a garage that closed. He's short-spoken, practical and in the middle politically, and he doesn't use AI tools. He's calm or uneasy in the milder pictures, counting on his spanners to keep him useful. AGI in 2 years alarms him because it takes both his farm job and his old trade, and he worries about his son, who wants to be a mechanic. With 5 years he saves and watches; with 10 he'd grudgingly retrain in machine wiring and hydraulics.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time to save or learn and his old mechanic's trade would go at the same time as the farm job.
whatWouldHelp: Some income while people find their feet, and proper hands-on courses for people who work with their hands rather than screen-based training.
